title: Turmeric Crosses Rs 23,000 a Quintal in Erode as Drought Cuts Planting
excerpt: Finger turmeric hit its highest level in recent years at Perundurai as drought in Maharashtra, Telangana and Tamil Nadu cut planted area by up to 30% in some regions and futures pointed to tight supplies into 2027.
body:
• Turmeric crossed Rs 23,000 a quintal at the Perundurai Regulated Market on October 14, with finger turmeric fetching Rs 15,336 to Rs 23,099 — its highest level in recent years, according to The Hindu.
  • Drought in Marathwada, Nizamabad and parts of Tamil Nadu has cut the area already planted by 20% to 30% in some regions, and traders expect a substantial fall in production next year.
  • April 2027 turmeric futures on NCDEX were trading between Rs 24,000 and Rs 25,000 a quintal, signalling that buyers expect tight supplies to last well beyond the current season.
  • For diaspora households, the practical takeaway is near-term cost: with fresh arrivals not expected until February 2027 and festival demand still running, retail turmeric powder and whole turmeric bought at Indian grocery stores are unlikely to get cheaper in the next few months — buying a normal household quantity now beats waiting for a price drop that traders do not see coming.

Turmeric prices crossed Rs 23,000 a quintal in Erode district this month, touching their highest level in recent years as lower arrivals, drought in major growing regions and uncertainty over the next crop tightened supplies. At the Perundurai Regulated Market on Wednesday, October 14, finger turmeric fetched between Rs 15,336 and Rs 23,099 a quintal, while bulb turmeric was priced between Rs 15,099 and Rs 19,626, The Hindu reported.

The pace of the rise is as notable as the level. At the Erode Regulated Market on October 7, finger turmeric had fetched between Rs 13,509 and Rs 19,244 a quintal. Within a week, the maximum price for finger turmeric rose by Rs 3,855 and the maximum for bulb turmeric by Rs 1,897. Other reporting from Erode puts the climb in a longer frame: prices have risen steadily from around Rs 15,000 a quintal at the start of September to above Rs 22,000 by mid-October.

Drought Is Cutting Both This Crop and the Next One

M. Sathyamurthy, secretary of the Erode Turmeric Merchants and Godown Owners' Association, told The Hindu that drought conditions in major turmeric-growing regions, including Marathwada in Maharashtra, Nizamabad in Telangana and parts of Tamil Nadu, were pushing up prices. The area already planted with turmeric had declined by 20% to 30% in some regions because of water scarcity, he said, with a further reduction in cultivation expected in the coming months.

"The drought impact is expected to be significant, leading to a substantial decline in production next year."

— M. Sathyamurthy, Erode Turmeric Merchants and Godown Owners' Association

Water is currently not being released from the Bhavanisagar dam for irrigation through the Lower Bhavani Project and Kalingarayan canals, whose command areas are major turmeric-growing regions. Mirror Now reported that drought in those same Lower Bhavani and Kalingarayan irrigation areas has already pushed some growers toward alternative crops, reducing cultivation while old stocks run down.

Why a Higher Price Does Not Automatically Help Farmers

A scarcity-driven price rise rewards only those who still have good stock to sell. The marketing season for freshly harvested turmeric generally runs from February to June, so many farmers will already have sold their crop before this rally. Those still holding quality stock may benefit, but they face storage charges, borrowing costs and quality deterioration while they wait, The Hawk reported in its analysis of the Erode market.

Drought also cuts both ways. It can reduce the quantity and quality of a harvest while farmers spend more on irrigation and labour, and a smaller crop must still cover nearly the same fixed expenses. The headline auction price is a top price for the best finger turmeric, not the rate every farmer receives after grading, moisture, transport and commission.

What It Means for Buyers and the Diaspora Kitchen

Turmeric is a daily cooking staple for Indian households, and festival-season demand rises further. Market participants cited by Mirror Now expect demand around Vijayadashami and Deepavali to sustain prices, while Erode's Geographical Indication-tagged turmeric keeps a premium in export markets. Wholesale increases in Erode do not translate instantly into a specific retail price abroad — that depends on inventories, processing and distribution margins — but they remove the case for expecting cheaper turmeric powder in the near term.

What to Watch Next

Two things will decide whether this rally extends. The first is weather: rainfall from the northeast monsoon, expected to set in this week, could help ease the water shortage, and Mr. Sathyamurthy said the crop situation in November and the impact of El Niño would influence prices in the coming months. The second is arrivals. Significant fresh supplies are not expected until February 2027, and some farmers who have stocked produce are reluctant to sell now in anticipation of further increases — behaviour that keeps near-term arrivals thin. Until one of those changes, turmeric remains a seller's market.
